extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature, literary critics, and translators interested in Cervantes and humour in Don Quixote
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative criteria the essay uses to judge Don Quixote and Cervantes' humour — what makes the book funny, effective, and enduring, and what pitfalls interpreters/illustrators/translators should avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vein of farce as primary popular ingredient
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredient which, more than its humour, or its wisdom, or the fertility of invention or knowledge of human nature it displays, has insured its success with the multitude, is the vein of farce that runs through it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the attack upon the sheep, the battle with the wine-skins, Mambrino’s helmet, Don Quixote knocked over by the sails of the windmill, Sancho tossed in the blanket. For general readers the farcical incidents were the main attraction and should be recognised as a central source of popular appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the great merits of 'Don Quixote'... is its simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity helps the book appeal to all classes of readers. Beware that some allusions are era- or locality-specific (e.g., Manchegan references) and may not strike modern or foreign readers immediately; but overall a simple style is a virtue and a source of universal accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of the incongruous (core comic mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cervantes’ humour is for the most part of that broader and simpler sort, the strength of which lies in the perception of the incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: the incongruity between Sancho and Don Quixote, Don Quixote’s chivalric ideals set against mean, prosaic surroundings (ventas, ugly windmills), and the mismatch of La Mancha as setting for knight-errantry. Recognising and foregrounding incongruity is key to understanding the book’s humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grave, matter-of-fact narrative voice / apparent unconsciousness of author
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the grave matter-of-factness of the narrative, and the apparent unconsciousness of the author that he is saying anything ludicrous, anything but the merest commonplace, that give its peculiar flavour to the humour of Cervantes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a flippant, self-conscious or facetious authorial tone when representing Cervantes; the humour works because the narrator 'leaves you alone with Don Quixote and Sancho' rather than signalling the joke to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of Sancho Panza (role and development)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sancho is an unconscious Mephistopheles, always unwittingly making mockery of his master’s aspirations... His lies are simple, homely, plump lies; plain working lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sancho was not in the original scheme but became essential. His stolid common-sense and homely mendacity are central comic elements; when assessing character, value authenticity and avoid turning him into mere caricature or exaggerated buffoonery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burlesque of the spirit of chivalry (not merely its incidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Second Part it is the spirit rather than the incidents of the chivalry romances that is the subject of the burlesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cervantes targets the exaggerated spirit — e.g., blind adoration of Dulcinea, transcendental idolatry of love — so critical readings or adaptations should focus on parodying the conventions and attitudes of romances, not just copying comic set-pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping Dulcinea in the background as a burlesque technique
rubrics_metrics.description: By keeping Dulcinea in the background, and making her a vague shadowy being of whose very existence we are left in doubt, he invests Don Quixote’s worship of her virtues and charms with an additional extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This deliberate absence intensifies the caricature of transcendental love; in adaptation or analysis, preserving Dulcinea's off-stage status preserves comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local colour / setting as interpretive key (La Mancha)
rubrics_metrics.description: La Mancha as the knight’s country and scene of his chivalries is of a piece with the pasteboard helmet... To anyone who knew the country well, the mere style and title of 'Don Quixote of La Mancha' gave the key to the author’s meaning at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the bleak, commonplace Manchegan landscape clarifies the author's ironic intent. Illustrators, translators, and readers should attend to the prosaic, ignoble features of setting to grasp the humour rooted in mismatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosaic surroundings used for contrast (mean details matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the mean, prosaic, commonplace character of all the surroundings and circumstances that gives a significance to Don Quixote’s vigil and the ceremony that follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast between high ceremonial aspiration and low, everyday reality is intentional; faithful representation of sordid or commonplace details enhances the irony and comic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of caricature / maintaining artistic restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: An inferior genius, taking him in hand a second time, would very likely have tried to improve him by making him more comical, clever, amiable, or virtuous. But Cervantes was too true an artist to spoil his work in this way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'improve' or over-enhance characters for cheap laughs; Cervantes refines rather than caricatures — preserving restraint and human truth is essential to maintain depth and humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial spontaneity / organic composition (limited premeditated plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: A very slight examination of the structure of 'Don Quixote' will suffice to show that Cervantes had no deep design or elaborate plan in his mind when he began the book... He had no idea of the goal to which his imagination was leading him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise the book’s partly improvised genesis (Sancho added later, division into chapters, invention of Cid Hamete) when evaluating structure: apparent looseness and episodic form are features, not necessarily flaws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to over-interpretation (caution against seeing deep allegory everywhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: To call 'Don Quixote' a sad book, preaching a pessimist view of life, argues a total misconception of its drift... To suppose Cervantes deliberately setting himself to expound any such idea in two stout quarto volumes is to suppose something not only very unlike the age in which he lived, but altogether unlike Cervantes himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid grand metaphysical or allegorical readings that impose systematic philosophies on the book; prefer explanations grounded in contemporary context and observable comic mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation and illustration challenges (loss of humour outside Spanish)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is true that to do full justice to Spanish humour in any other language is well-nigh an impossibility... Sancho Panza’s drollery... lose[s] half their flavour when transferred from their native Castilian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators must be aware that Spanish's natural gravity and sonorous stateliness contribute to the comic effect; illustrators unfamiliar with Spanish settings risk missing the point (example: Doré's elaborate fountain misses the mean venta). Faithful, context-aware rendering is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual/editorial fidelity affects critical reception
rubrics_metrics.description: All the editions printed in Spain from 1637 to 1771... were mere trade editions, badly and carelessly printed... The London edition of 1738... produced 'Don Quixote' in becoming form as regards paper and type, and... aimed at correctness of text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful editing and correct text selection matter; poor printings and chap-book style can encourage dismissal of the work as mere drollery, while conscientious editing raises its critical status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect arises from character-relational dynamics (Don Quixote ≠ source of nobility)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the First Part, Don Quixote has no character or individuality... It was the business of a knight-errant to right wrongs... Of all Byron’s melodious nonsense about Don Quixote, the most nonsensical statement is that '’tis his virtue makes him mad!' The exact opposite is the truth; it is his madness makes him virtuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Don Quixote, emphasise how the comic situation and his delusions produce apparent virtues; avoid romanticized readings that attribute a prior nobility to the character independent of his madness.
